newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Romanian troops bring relief to Albanian town.
newsitem.headline: Romanian troops bring relief to Albanian town.

text.p: Romanian troops began setting up camp outside this troubled Albanian border town on Tuesday to the relief of residents terrified by growing lawlessness.

Nearly 400 Romanian soldiers, part of the eight-nation United Nations approved force sent to Albania to secure aid supplies, are due to arrive over the next two days to secure the area around Gjirokaster, 30 kms (20 miles) from the Greek border.
"When the multi-national force took control of the port of Vlore, they stopped the smuggling. The same sort of thing may happen here," Gjirokaster mayor Ylli Asllani told Reuters.

While the mandate given to the 6,000 troops does not allow them to disarm Albanians or to act as a police force, residents hope their simple presence will cool the emotions of newly armed young hoodlums who are making the streets of the town their battleground.

"We haven't received our specific instructions from Tirana yet. We will need a week to 10 days to get established but our troops will be doing their job throughout the area," Major Calin Hentea, a spokesman for the Romanian troops told Reuters.
Asllani said security was everyone's top priority.
"We don't need flour here, we need security," said Asllani, referring to over 1,000 tonnes of wheat flour shipped in for distribution as humanitarian relief by the multi-national force.
Police complain that without assistance they cannot control the wave of violent crime.

The cafe next to police headquarters is riddled with bullet holes, and the police wages delivery requires an escort of four cars bristling with Kalashnikovs. An armoured personnel carrier guarded the station on Tuesday as old people arrived to collect their pensions.

Local hospital director Dr Hodo Cela said his team had seen 326 firearms wounds in the past two months, where before there was seldom one a month. There have been 11 deaths in the town of 30,000 and 24 serious injuries have been evacuated to specialist hospitals in neighbouring Greece.

His staff have been constantly intimidated by threats, often from the barrel of a Kalashnikov, made by relatives and friends of the wounded. A Reuter vehicle outside the hospital was robbed of its radio speakers, and the driver threatened with a gun, as this reporter was interviewing the director.

Gjirokaster, the home of many of Albania's ethnic Greek minority, was a focus of the rioting that swept Albania in March following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in which many lost their life savings.

The town's smart new hotel and shopping complex, owned by Gjallica, the company that ran one of the main pyramid schemes, was torched and gutted in the riots, and mayor Asllani said 25 public buildings were destroyed.

Hundreds of soldiers deserted the army barracks, headquarters of Albania's southern infantry, artillery and tanks division, and locals looted several military arsenals in the area, distributing thousands of weapons among the population.

Schools have been closed since President Sali Berisha declared emergency rule in early March to halt the nation's drift towards anarchy, and many teenagers have whiled away the hours playing with their newly acquired weapons.
"It makes us all very angry because it is the children that are suffering," said teacher Angjelina Kola. "Perhaps the foreign troops could help with collecting up the weapons."
